# Purpose and assumed background {.unnumbered}

This is the first note in the sequence. It assumes only familiar probability,
algebra, and basic calculus. It does **not** assume measure theory, real
analysis, topology, or abstract algebra.

Its main purpose is to make the formula

$$
P_X=P\circ X^{-1}
$$

completely readable. The symbol $\circ$ is pronounced “composed with.” The
symbol $X^{-1}$ means an **inverse image of a set** here; it does not require
the random variable $X$ to have an inverse function.

# 1. Sets are collections of objects

A **set** is a collection of objects. Braces list its members. For example,

$$
A=\{1,3,5\}.
$$

Basic notation is:

| Notation | Read it as | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| $x\in A$ | $x$ is in $A$ | $x$ is a member of $A$ |
| $x\notin A$ | $x$ is not in $A$ | $x$ is not a member of $A$ |
| $A\subseteq B$ | $A$ is a subset of $B$ | Every member of $A$ is also in $B$ |
| $A=B$ | $A$ equals $B$ | The two sets have exactly the same members |
| $\emptyset$ | the empty set | The set with no members |
| $\{x\}$ | the singleton containing $x$ | A set containing one object |

The order in which elements are listed does not matter, and repeated listings
do not create new elements:

$$
\{1,3,5\}=\{5,1,3\}=\{1,1,3,5\}.
$$

## The underlying or sample set

In probability, $\Omega$ denotes the set of all elementary outcomes. If an
experiment consists of tossing a coin twice, one possible choice is

$$
\Omega=\{HH,HT,TH,TT\}.
$$

An **event** is a subset of $\Omega$. For example,

$$
A=\{HH,HT,TH\}
$$

is the event “at least one head occurs.”

## The power set

The **power set** $\mathcal P(\Omega)$ is the set of all subsets of $\Omega$.
For $\Omega=\{H,T\}$,

$$
\mathcal P(\Omega)
=\{\emptyset,\{H\},\{T\},\{H,T\}\}.
$$

The notation is one level higher than it first appears:

- $H$ is an outcome;
- $\{H\}$ is a set of outcomes, hence an event;
- $\mathcal P(\Omega)$ is a set whose members are events.

Later, a sigma-field $\mathcal F$ will be a selected collection of events, so
$\mathcal F\subseteq\mathcal P(\Omega)$.

One notation warning: $\mathcal P(\Omega)$ conventionally means the power set
in elementary set theory. Bayesian nonparametric writing also often uses
$\mathcal P(\mathcal X)$ for the **set of probability measures** on
$\mathcal X$. Those are different collections; the surrounding definition
determines which meaning is intended.

# 2. Operations on sets

Let $A$ and $B$ be subsets of $\Omega$.

| Operation | Notation | Membership rule |
|---|---|---|
| Union | $A\cup B$ | In $A$, in $B$, or in both |
| Intersection | $A\cap B$ | In both $A$ and $B$ |
| Complement | $A^c$ | In $\Omega$ but not in $A$ |
| Difference | $A\setminus B$ | In $A$ but not in $B$ |

For

$$
\Omega=\{1,2,3,4\},\qquad
A=\{1,2,3\},\qquad B=\{3,4\},
$$

we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
A\cup B&=\{1,2,3,4\},\\
A\cap B&=\{3\},\\
A^c&=\{4\},\\
A\setminus B&=\{1,2\}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Sets $A$ and $B$ are **disjoint** if $A\cap B=\emptyset$. They cannot both
occur.

## Indexed collections

The notation $A_1,A_2,\ldots$ describes a sequence of sets. Then

$$
\bigcup_{j=1}^{\infty}A_j
$$

means all points belonging to at least one $A_j$, while

$$
\bigcap_{j=1}^{\infty}A_j
$$

means all points belonging to every $A_j$.

“Countable” means that the objects can be placed in a finite or infinite list
indexed by $1,2,3,\ldots$. The integers are countable; the real line is
uncountable.

# 3. Functions map inputs to outputs

A function written

$$
X:\Omega\longrightarrow\mathcal X
$$

takes each input $\omega\in\Omega$ and assigns exactly one output
$X(\omega)\in\mathcal X$.

- $\Omega$ is the **domain**, the set of allowed inputs.
- $\mathcal X$ is the **codomain**, the set in which outputs take values.
- $X(\omega)$ is the output associated with input $\omega$.

The function need not be one-to-one. Several inputs may have the same output.

## Example: number of heads

Let

$$
\Omega=\{HH,HT,TH,TT\}
$$

and define $X$ to be the number of heads. Then

| $\omega$ | $X(\omega)$ |
|---|---:|
| $HH$ | 2 |
| $HT$ | 1 |
| $TH$ | 1 |
| $TT$ | 0 |

Thus $X:\Omega\to\{0,1,2\}$. Notice that $HT$ and $TH$ both map to 1.

# 4. The inverse image of a set

Suppose $B$ is a set of possible outputs, $B\subseteq\mathcal X$. The
**inverse image** or **preimage** of $B$ under $X$ is

$$
\boxed{
X^{-1}(B)=\{\omega\in\Omega:X(\omega)\in B\}.
}
\tag{1}
$$

It is the set of inputs whose outputs land in $B$.

In the coin example, let $B=\{1,2\}$. Then

> Which elementary outcomes would make $X$ fall in $B$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

Check the table one elementary outcome at a time and retain the outcomes for
which $X(\omega)\in\{1,2\}$. This gives

$$
X^{-1}(B)=\{HH,HT,TH\},
$$

because those are exactly the outcomes producing at least one head. The outcome
$TT$ is excluded because $X(TT)=0\notin B$.
:::

## This is not an inverse function

An inverse function would take one output and recover one unique input. That is
impossible here because both $HT$ and $TH$ produce $X=1$.

An inverse **image**, however, always makes sense:

$$
X^{-1}(\{1\})=\{HT,TH\}.
$$

Therefore the notation $X^{-1}(B)$ in probability does not claim that $X$ is
invertible. It asks for all inputs whose outputs belong to the specified set.

## Useful inverse-image rules

Inverse images preserve the set operations needed in probability:

$$
\begin{aligned}
X^{-1}(B^c)&=\bigl[X^{-1}(B)\bigr]^c,\\
X^{-1}\left(\bigcup_jB_j\right)&=\bigcup_jX^{-1}(B_j),\\
X^{-1}\left(\bigcap_jB_j\right)&=\bigcap_jX^{-1}(B_j).
\end{aligned}
$$

This is why inverse images, rather than ordinary images, appear in the
definition of a measurable random variable.

# 5. A random variable is a function with a probability-compatible property

A probability measure $P$ assigns probabilities to events in a sigma-field
$\mathcal F$ on $\Omega$. Suppose $\mathscr X$ is the collection of events we
want to discuss in the output space $\mathcal X$.

For the moment, read “sigma-field” as the declared collection of allowable
events. The next note gives its three formal closure rules.

The function $X:\Omega\to\mathcal X$ is **measurable** when

$$
B\in\mathscr X
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
X^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal F.
\tag{2}
$$

Equation (2) says that every output-space question we permit can be translated
back into an input-space event to which $P$ can assign a probability.

In elementary statistics this condition is usually invisible because familiar
functions on familiar spaces are measurable. Its purpose is to rule out
pathological functions for which $P\{X\in B\}$ would not be defined.

# 6. From the probability of outcomes to the distribution of X

The underlying measure $P$ knows probabilities of events in $\Omega$. We want
a measure $P_X$ that knows probabilities of events in the value space
$\mathcal X$.

For $B\subseteq\mathcal X$, define

$$
\boxed{
P_X(B)=P\bigl(X^{-1}(B)\bigr)=P(X\in B).
}
\tag{3}
$$

This $P_X$ is the **distribution** or **law** of $X$.

In the fair-coin example,

$$
\begin{aligned}
P_X(\{1\})
&=P\bigl(X^{-1}(\{1\})\bigr)\\
&=P(\{HT,TH\})\\
&=\frac12.
\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly,

$$
P_X(\{0\})=\frac14,
\qquad
P_X(\{2\})=\frac14.
$$

# 7. Decoding the composition formula

Equation (3) is abbreviated as

$$
\boxed{P_X=P\circ X^{-1}.}
\tag{4}
$$

Function composition is normally defined by

$$
(g\circ f)(z)=g\bigl(f(z)\bigr).
$$

Read it from right to left: first apply $f$, then apply $g$.

In (4), the input is a set $B$ in the value space:

$$
\begin{aligned}
(P\circ X^{-1})(B)
&=P\bigl(X^{-1}(B)\bigr).
\end{aligned}
$$

The two stages are:

1. $X^{-1}$ turns the output event $B$ into an event in $\Omega$.
2. $P$ assigns a probability to that event.

Thus $P\circ X^{-1}$ is not multiplication, and $P$ is not being evaluated at
a number. The composition creates a new set function on the value space.

# 8. Why it is called a pushforward

The measure $P_X$ is called the **pushforward** of $P$ through $X$. One writes

$$
P_X=X_{\#}P
$$

in some texts; $P\circ X^{-1}$ is more common in probability.

The name describes a change of viewpoint:

| Level | Objects receiving probability |
|---|---|
| $P$ on $\Omega$ | Elementary outcomes $\omega$ |
| $P_X$ on $\mathcal X$ | Values $x=X(\omega)$ |

Probability mass is not physically moved. The same uncertainty is being
reported in terms of the derived quantity $X$ rather than the hidden outcome
$\omega$.

## The familiar CDF is built from the pushforward

For a real-valued random variable,

$$
F_X(x)
=P(X\leq x)
=P_X\bigl((-\infty,x]\bigr).
$$

Therefore the CDF, PMF, and PDF you already use describe the pushforward
distribution $P_X$, usually without mentioning the underlying $\Omega$.

# 9. Indicator functions translate membership into numbers

For a set $A$, its **indicator function** is

$$
\mathbf 1_A(x)
=
\begin{cases}
1,&x\in A,\\
0,&x\notin A.
\end{cases}
$$

Equivalent notations include $I(x\in A)$ and $\mathbf 1(x\in A)$.

Indicators connect events with expectations:

$$
E\{\mathbf 1_A(X)\}=P(X\in A).
$$

They also connect sets with integration. For any measure $\mu$,

$$
\int\mathbf 1_A(x)\,\mu(dx)=\mu(A).
$$

The later measure and integration notes develop this identity.

# 10. Points, functions, and functionals

The input to an ordinary function may be a number:

$$
h:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R,\qquad h(x)=x^2.
$$

The input can also be an entire function or probability distribution. A
function whose input is itself a function or distribution is often called a
**functional**.

Examples include

$$
T(F)=\int xF(dx)
$$

for the mean of distribution $F$, and

$$
H(f)=\int f(x)^2dx
$$

for an integrated feature of density $f$.

The integrals are only examples of the input-output type; the following notes
explain $F(dx)$ and $dx$ themselves. At this stage, the key point is that one
entire $F$ or $f$, rather than a single number, is supplied as the input.

This terminology matters in Bayesian nonparametrics because the “points” in
the model space may be entire distributions. A prior can then assign
probability to sets of such points.

# 11. A notation ladder

| Expression | Type of object | Plain-language reading |
|---|---|---|
| $\omega$ | Point in $\Omega$ | One elementary outcome |
| $A\subseteq\Omega$ | Set | An event |
| $P(A)$ | Number | Probability of the event |
| $X(\omega)$ | Point in $\mathcal X$ | Observed value produced by $\omega$ |
| $B\subseteq\mathcal X$ | Set | A set of possible observed values |
| $X^{-1}(B)$ | Set in $\Omega$ | Outcomes that produce a value in $B$ |
| $P_X(B)$ | Number | Probability that $X$ falls in $B$ |
| $P_X=P\circ X^{-1}$ | Equality of measures | The law of $X$ is the pushforward of $P$ |

Continue to [Measure and probability foundations](measure-probability-foundations.qmd).

# Check your understanding

For the two-coin example, answer the following before continuing.

Select each **Answer** box after working out the question yourself.

**1. What are the domain and codomain of $X$?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

The domain is the elementary-outcome space
$\Omega=\{HH,HT,TH,TT\}$. The codomain used in this example is
$\mathcal X=\{0,1,2\}$, the possible numbers of heads. Thus
$X:\Omega\to\mathcal X$.
:::

**2. Find $X^{-1}(\{0,2\})$.**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

$X(TT)=0$ and $X(HH)=2$, while the other two outcomes map to 1. Therefore

$$
X^{-1}(\{0,2\})=\{TT,HH\}.
$$
:::

**3. Why does $X^{-1}$ make sense even though $X$ is not one-to-one?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

Here $X^{-1}(B)$ is an **inverse image of a set**, not an inverse function. It
collects every input $\omega$ satisfying $X(\omega)\in B$. Several inputs may
therefore appear in the same inverse image; uniqueness is not required.
:::

**4. Expand $(P\circ X^{-1})(\{1\})$ into two steps.**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

First take the inverse image,

$$
X^{-1}(\{1\})=\{HT,TH\}.
$$

Then apply $P$. For two fair, independent coin tosses,

$$
(P\circ X^{-1})(\{1\})=P(\{HT,TH\})=\frac12.
$$
:::

**5. What is the difference between $P$ and $P_X$?**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

$P$ assigns probabilities to events in the elementary-outcome space $\Omega$.
$P_X$ assigns probabilities to sets of values in $\mathcal X$. They are linked
by $P_X(B)=P\{X^{-1}(B)\}$.
:::

**6. Evaluate $E\{\mathbf 1_{\{1,2\}}(X)\}$ for fair coins.**

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

An indicator's expectation is the probability of its event, so

$$
E\{\mathbf 1_{\{1,2\}}(X)\}
=P(X\in\{1,2\})
=P(\{HH,HT,TH\})
=\frac34.
$$
:::
